implementation_notes: POSIX threads supply the reusable barrier directly: pthread_barrier_init(&b, NULL, parties) fixes the party count, every worker calls pthread_barrier_wait(), and the call returns PTHREAD_BARRIER_SERIAL_THREAD to exactly one unspecified thread - a free leader hook for phase-local work - and zero to the rest; the barrier resets itself after each release, so one object serves all generations. There is no one-shot latch in the standard: compose it from a mutex plus a condition variable (decrement a counter, broadcast when it reaches zero, and broadcast again on the failure path), or use a counting semaphore when the waiters are also the completers. Compiling against POSIX requires _POSIX_C_SOURCE or _XOPEN_SOURCE to be defined before <pthread.h>, and not every platform implements pthread_barrier_t (macOS historically did not), which is exactly when the mutex plus condition-variable form earns its keep.
pitfalls: Only two return values mean success (PTHREAD_BARRIER_SERIAL_THREAD and 0) and an interrupted wait resumes waiting rather than failing, so any timeout or abort must come from the application, not from the call.

There is no built-in liveness protection: if one worker exits or never reaches the barrier the rest block forever, so worker death must be signalled through a side channel and the wait must be followed by a check of that channel.
pthread_barrier_t is not portable to every POSIX platform and needs the feature-test macro in place before <pthread.h>; otherwise the type is simply not declared and the build fails late.
